subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does 'decomposition' mean in computational thinking?
options: Breaking a large problem down into smaller, more manageable sub-problems
Removing unnecessary detail from a problem
Writing a solution as a flowchart
Testing a program to find errors
questions.explain: Decomposition splits a complex problem into smaller sub-problems that are easier to solve individually.

options: Removing or hiding unnecessary detail to focus on the important parts
Splitting a task into repeated steps
Ordering data from smallest to largest
Combining two Boolean values
questions.explain: Abstraction hides irrelevant detail so that only the information needed to solve the problem is considered.

questions.q: Which condition must be true for a binary search to work correctly?
options: The list must already be sorted into order
The list must contain only numbers
The list must have an even number of items
The list must be stored in a two-dimensional array
questions.explain: Binary search relies on the data being ordered so it can repeatedly discard half of the remaining items.

questions.q: In a bubble sort, which items are compared during each step of a pass?
options: Adjacent (neighbouring) items
The first and last items only
The middle item and the first item
Two randomly chosen items
questions.explain: A bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent pairs of items and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.

questions.q: For a two-input AND operation, when is the output equal to 1 (true)?
options: Only when both inputs are 1
When at least one input is 1
When both inputs are 0
When the two inputs are different
questions.explain: An AND operation outputs 1 only when every input is 1, otherwise it outputs 0.

questions.q: What does a NOT operation do to its single input?
options: Inverts it, so 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0
Leaves the input unchanged
Outputs 1 only if the input is 1
Combines it with a second input
questions.explain: NOT is a unary operation that inverts (negates) its input.

questions.q: For a two-input OR operation, when is the output equal to 0 (false)?
options: Only when both inputs are 0
When at least one input is 1
When both inputs are 1
When the inputs are different
questions.explain: OR outputs 1 if at least one input is 1, so it only outputs 0 when both inputs are 0.

questions.q: Which sorting algorithm works by repeatedly splitting the list into halves and then merging them back together in order?
options: Merge sort
Bubble sort
Linear search
Binary search
questions.explain: Merge sort uses a divide-and-conquer approach, splitting the list into halves and merging sorted sub-lists.

questions.q: Why can a linear search be used on an unsorted list when a binary search cannot?
options: A linear search checks each item in turn, so order does not matter
A linear search sorts the list first
A linear search only works on numbers
A linear search always starts from the middle item
questions.explain: Linear search inspects each element sequentially, so the data does not need to be in any order.

questions.q: For a large sorted list, why is a binary search generally more efficient than a linear search?
options: It halves the remaining items to check with each comparison
It checks every item twice as fast
It never needs any comparisons
It always finds the item on the first attempt
questions.explain: Each binary search comparison discards half of the remaining data, so far fewer items need checking.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a benefit of decomposing a problem before writing a program?
options: Smaller sub-problems can be solved and tested separately, making the task easier to manage
It guarantees the program contains no logic errors
It removes the need to write any algorithms
It automatically sorts the program's data
questions.explain: Decomposition lets each sub-problem be tackled and tested independently, and work can be shared between people.

questions.q: A railway map shows lines and stations but not the true distances or streets. This is an example of which computational thinking technique?
options: Abstraction
Decomposition
Iteration
Sorting
questions.explain: The map is an abstraction because unnecessary detail is removed, leaving only the information a passenger needs.

questions.q: How many rows of input combinations does a truth table for a logic expression with two inputs have?
questions.explain: With two inputs there are 2 to the power 2 = 4 possible combinations of 0s and 1s.

questions.q: How many rows of input combinations does a truth table with three inputs have?
questions.explain: With three inputs there are 2 to the power 3 = 8 possible input combinations.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of comparisons a linear search needs to search a list of n items?
options: n
n divided by 2
2 to the power n
questions.explain: In the worst case the target is the last item or absent, so all n items must be checked.

questions.q: Using a binary search on the sorted list [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13], how many comparisons are needed to find the value 11?
questions.explain: The middle value 7 is checked first (11 is greater), then 11 is the middle of the right half, so 2 comparisons are needed.

questions.q: A bubble sort arranges the list [5, 3, 8, 1] into ascending order. What is the list after the first complete pass?
questions.explain: Swapping 5 and 3, keeping 5 and 8, then swapping 8 and 1 gives [3, 5, 1, 8] after the first pass.

questions.q: If A = 1 and B = 0, what is the result of the expression A AND (NOT B)?
options: Cannot be determined
Both 0 and 1
questions.explain: NOT B is 1, and 1 AND 1 evaluates to 1.

questions.q: What is the result of the expression NOT (1 OR 0)?
options: Undefined
questions.explain: 1 OR 0 evaluates to 1, and NOT 1 gives 0.
